query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: For equiatomic (or near‐equiatomic) multimetal nanoparticles initially in a single-phase solid solution, kinetic limitations on surface atomic diffusion—not simply the thermodynamic stabilization of the high-entropy phase—govern whether the structure and chemical composition are maintained under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions (473–1923 K). A surface kinetic barrier (such as provided by an encapsulating layer) can slow down atomic rearrangements and dissolution that would otherwise lead to phase segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and crystallized as a single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Expose nanoparticles to high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions while comparing samples with and without an externally imposed kinetic barrier (for example, by adding a thin encapsulating layer such as graphene).
generation.conditions: Under inert or controlled atmospheres that mimic catalytic/thermoelectric environments, with temperatures ramped within the 473–1923 K range and identical operational protocols for both the modified and unmodified nanoparticles.
generation.structural_mediator: The kinetics of surface atomic diffusion, which influences elemental segregation and surface dissolution.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the intrinsic atomic mobility tends to promote surface diffusion and elemental migration that can lead to phase separation or chemical degradation. However, if a kinetic barrier (e.g., a graphene shell) is present, the slower diffusion kinetics will preserve the solid solution structure. Thus, even if the thermodynamic driving forces might favor segregation at high temperatures, the rate at which it occurs is governed by kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with an imposed kinetic barrier (e.g., graphene encapsulation) will show a slower rate of elemental segregation and dissolution, preserving their single-phase structure and catalytic/thermoelectric performance, compared to unmodified nanoparticles which will exhibit faster degradation in structure and performance.
generation.baseline: The as-synthesized equiatomic solid solution nanoparticles characterized at lower temperatures before exposure to high-temperature operating conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under conditions where surface diffusion is the primary pathway for structural and chemical change, and it may not hold if external chemical reactions (e.g., oxidation in strongly reactive atmospheres) or abrupt phase transitions dominate the behavior.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how factors such as intrinsic lattice distortions or possible synergistic effects between elements under extreme conditions might interact with the kinetic barriers. Also, the relative roles of other degradation pathways (e.g., bulk diffusion or chemical reactions not mitigated by surface encapsulation) are not fully defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles with identical equiatomic, single-phase compositions: one set with a surface encapsulation layer (e.g., graphene) and one without. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature catalytic/thermoelectric operating conditions within the range of 473–1923 K in a controlled inert atmosphere. Periodically analyze the nanoparticles using in-situ X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with elemental mapping (EDS), and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) to monitor phase purity, elemental segregation, and dissolution rates.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the encapsulated and non-encapsulated nanoparticles exhibit similar rates of phase segregation, elemental migration, and degradation in catalytic/thermoelectric performance under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that kinetic barriers control the high-temperature stability would be falsified.

## Abstract
SummaryHigh-entropy alloys are claimed to possess superior stability due to thermodynamic contributions. However, this statement mostly lies on a hypothetical basis. In this study, we use on-line inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer to investigate the dissolution of five representative electrocatalysts in acidic and alkaline media and a wide potential window targeting the most important applications. To address both model and applied systems, we synthesized thin films and carbon-supported nanoparticles ranging from an elemental (Pt) sample to binary (PtRu), ternary (PtRuIr), quaternary (PtRuIrRh), and quinary (PtRuIrRhPd) alloy samples. For certain metals in the high-entropy alloy under alkaline conditions, lower dissolution was observed. Still, the improvement was not striking and can be rather explained by the lowered concentration of elements in the multinary alloys instead of the synergistic effects of thermodynamics. We postulate that this is because of dissolution kinetic effects, which are always present under electrocatalytic conditions, overcompensating thermodynamic contributions. ## Abstract
AbstractRapid synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA NPs) offers new opportunities to develop functional materials in widespread applications. Although some methods have successfully produced HEA NPs, these methods generally require rigorous conditions such as high pressure, high temperature, restricted atmosphere, and limited substrates, which impede practical viability. In this work, we report laser solid-phase synthesis of CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticles by laser irradiation of mixed metal precursors on a laser-induced graphene (LIG) support with a 3D porous structure. The CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticles are embraced by several graphene layers, forming graphene shell-encapsulated HEA nanoparticles. The mechanisms of the laser solid-phase synthesis of HEA NPs on LIG supports are investigated through theoretical simulation and experimental observations, in consideration of mixed metal precursor adsorption, thermal decomposition, reduction through electrons from laser-induced thermionic emission, and liquid beads splitting.
